title: Oto-Manguean languages - Wikipedia
text: The highest number of speakers of Oto-Manguean languages today is in the Mexican state of Oaxaca, where the two largest branches, the Zapotecan and the Mixtecan languages, are spoken by almost 1.5 million people combined.

title: Mixtec languages - Wikipedia
text: Through music or the way in which certain rituals are carried out, popular Mixtec literature has survived as it did for millennia: by means of oral transmission.

title: Mixtec, Itundujia Language (MCE) – L1 & L2 Speakers, Status ...
text: Itundujia Mixtec is an endangered indigenous language of Mexico. It belongs to the Otomanguean language family. The language is used as a first language by adults only. It is not known to be taught in schools.

title: A Mixtec Sound Change Database - Journal of Open Humanities Data
text: We present an interlinked, expandable database of segmental sound changes among a large sample of Mixtec languages of Mexico. The database provides an up-to-date repository for scholars working on Mixtec and related languages.

title: Música mixteca - UCLA Library Digital Collections
text: SPANISH: Grabación en vivo del grupo musical conocido como Los Amigos y de la Banda de San Martín de las Palmas. La grabación se realizó en el municipio de Santiago Tilantongo, Oaxaca y es una muestra de la música típica de la mixteca. Algunas canciones son interpretadas en mixteco.

title: Mixtec culture
text: We hope these pages will show you more about the history, arts, literature and music of the region. The Mixtec is found in the mountains of Puebla, Oaxaca and Guerrero states and its territories range from deep forest, humid coastlands to lush valleys.

title: Mixtec Sound Change Database 2.0: Integrating Tone Change
text: This paper introduces and describes the second edition of the Mixtec Sound Change Database (Auderset & Campbell, 2024), which now includes a module on tone change.
